items.rationale: The narrative itself cites established literature describing cutaneous reactions to this drug class.
items.evidence_text: Cutaneous reactions to this drug class are well described in the published literature

items.rationale: The first dose was taken on 2 March and the rash appeared on 5 March.
items.evidence_text: She took the first dose on the morning of 2 March

items.rationale: The rash fully resolved after the drug was withdrawn.
items.evidence_text: The rash faded over four days and had fully resolved by 9 March

items.rationale: An inadvertent rechallenge reproduced the rash within twelve hours in the same distribution. This is the strongest single piece of evidence in the case.
items.evidence_text: the maculopapular rash recurred within twelve hours, again affecting the trunk and upper arms

items.rationale: The narrative positively excludes the main alternatives: no other medications and no significant medical history. This is documented absence rather than mere silence.
items.evidence_text: She was taking no other medications

items.rationale: No placebo was administered, as is normal outside a controlled trial.
No drug concentrations were measured. For a cutaneous hypersensitivity reaction these would not be expected to be informative.
No dose escalation or reduction is described, so no dose-response relationship can be assessed.
The patient reported a rash to a sulfonamide-containing antibiotic as a teenager, a structurally related agent.
items.evidence_text: she had developed a rash after a sulfonamide-containing antibiotic as a teenager

items.rationale: The rash was observed by a clinician on examination and photographed in the clinical record.
items.evidence_text: documented on examination by her general practitioner and photographed in the clinical record
